articleHeadline: Chinese surveillance shows steep declines in reported vector-borne diseases
articleSummary: Five vector-borne diseases in China—typhus, dengue, leishmaniasis, malaria, and epidemic encephalitis B (EEB)—showed substantially lower reported incidence and deaths in 2020–2023 than 2013–2019. Overall incidence declined by 59.86% (95% CI -60.36% to -59.36%; P<0.001) and mortality by 83.72% (95% CI -87.86% to -78.18%; P<0.001). The analysis used province- and age-specific surveillance data for 2004–2020 from the Chinese CDC and national aggregate data for 2021–2023 from the National Health Commission; national trends extend through 2023. Malaria and EEB had the largest reductions; typhus and leishmaniasis were less affected. Southern provinces hosted most spatial hotspots in earlier periods. Methods included Joinpoint regression, STL seasonal-trend decomposition, interrupted time-series analysis, and SARIMA forecasts. The authors caution against attributing declines solely to COVID-19 measures, noting possible contributions from longer-term trends, control programs, and reporting changes, and call for reliable surveillance and adaptable forecasting.

articleSummary: Seasonal influenza circulating year-round in Vietnam poses variable seasonal surges, with most infections mild and self-limiting. High-risk groups for severe illness include people aged 65 and older, children under 5, pregnant women (especially in the last trimester or within two weeks postpartum), and individuals with chronic conditions such as cardiovascular or chronic lung disease, kidney disease, liver disease, diabetes, or immune suppression. Transmission occurs mainly via respiratory droplets from coughing, sneezing, or talking, with elevated risk in crowded, poorly ventilated places, schools, healthcare facilities, and on public transport. Preventive measures urged by Vietnam's Department of Preventive Medicine, Ministry of Health, include wearing masks in health facilities, public transport, and crowded or poorly ventilated spaces; covering coughs/sneezes; hand hygiene; avoiding touching the face; maintaining ventilation; and staying home when symptomatic. Those at risk should limit exposure and seek medical advice promptly; avoid self-medication with antivirals or antibiotics without professional guidance.

articleSummary: West China Hospital, southwestern China, conducted a retrospective single-centre study of 1,999 patients with confirmed pulmonary TB who underwent bronchoscopy between September 2013 and June 2019. Of these, 439 (22.0%) were diagnosed with tracheobronchial tuberculosis (TBTB), and among them 218 (49.7%) developed airway stenosis. Multivariable analysis identified three independent predictors of TBTB: female sex (odds ratio [OR] 5.726; 95% CI 1.913–17.133; p=0.002), age <50 years (OR 4.144; 95% CI 1.791–9.588; p=0.001), and positive sputum acid-fast smear (OR 2.494; 95% CI 0.998–6.636; p=0.050). However, CIs are wide and near 1 for the smear, reflecting uncertainty; associations describe relationships within the bronchoscopy-selected cohort rather than causality. Among TBTB patients, 218 (49.7%) developed airway stenosis. Timing and outcomes of stenosis were not detailed, and results cannot be extrapolated to unselected TB populations.

articleSummary: Influenza A complications arise when the virus directly injures lung tissue or when bacterial superinfection or preexisting conditions worsen disease. articleHeadline: Two novel Silviavirus phages with lytic activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: genomic and phenotypic characterization
articleSummary: Two novel Silviavirus bacteriophages, CARØ0038 and CARØ0046, isolated from sewage in Davangere, Karnataka, India, lyse methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Genome sizes are 120,939 bp and 136,667 bp, encoding 227 and 225 predicted proteins with GC contents of 29.5% and 29.1%, respectively; phylogenomics place them in genus Silviavirus with unclear species-level assignment. Host range includes all 28 tested MRSA isolates and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus; no lysis of S. epidermidis or S. saprophyticus under tested conditions. articleSummary: Global travel regions report rising dengue fever cases in parts of Brazil, Cuba, the Philippines, and Florida, prompting the Centers for Travel Medicine (CRM) to issue precautionary guidance for tourists. Many infections are asymptomatic; when present, symptoms include high fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, retro-orbital eye pain, and rash. Incubation is typically 4–7 days, up to two weeks in some cases; a minority progress to severe disease with abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and mucosal bleeding. Protection is essential: seek pre-travel medical advice, assess personal risk, and consider vaccination (though STIKO currently recommends vaccination only after a first confirmed infection; others criticize this stance). articleSummary: Rain-driven Aedes mosquitoes in monsoon cities such as Chennai spread dengue, chikungunya and Zika, which share early symptoms but require lab confirmation. Dengue often features severe body aches, eye pain, falling platelets and possible abdominal pain, vomiting or bleeding as warning signs; risk of complications rises as fever subsides. Chikungunya presents with sudden high fever and intense joint pain, swelling and stiffness—wrists, fingers, knees, ankles—with possible prolonged stiffness after fever ends. Zika tends to be milder, may cause rash, red eyes and joint pains, but is concerning for pregnant women due to potential fetal brain impact; testing is advised for any fever with rash in pregnancy. Because symptoms overlap, doctors rely on travel history, local outbreak patterns, day of illness, and blood tests (molecular or antibody) to confirm. Home care: fluids; avoid aspirin/ibuprofen until dengue is ruled out. Seek hospital same day if bleeding, vomiting, or severe abdominal pain.

articleSummary: Hyderabad-based CSIR-CCMB researchers identify DZIP3 as a dual-function sensor and activator of the human antiviral response. articleHeadline: Large-scale meteorological patterns linked to Ebola virus outbreaks
articleSummary: Ebola outbreaks are linked to large-scale meteorological patterns rather than random timing, a University of Malaga-led study finds. Outbreaks in Central Africa, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, correlate with distant climate oscillations (teleconnections). As of Sept. 26, 2026, the latest outbreak has >8,000 confirmed infections and 3,901 deaths (case fatality rate ~50%), with the outbreak beginning in May. Analyzing 49 outbreaks (1976–2025) against 26 climate indices, the researchers identify four signals associated with outbreak distribution: the Caribbean Sea Surface Temperature Index (CAR; not available since Feb 2020), the Dipole Mode Index (IMD), the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO), and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), the latter being the most frequent predictor. They caution these indices do not cause Ebola but may indicate environmental conditions conducive to outbreaks, offering a six-to-twelve month warning window. The work—co-authored by UMA, the Spanish Institute of Oceanography, Manchester Metropolitan University, and CIFOR—appears in Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment (Springer Nature) as a surveillance tool for preparedness.

The findings, published in The EMBO Journal, indicate protection against multiple viruses, including SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), chikungunya, and Japanese encephalitis virus. The work deepens understanding of innate immunity and points to potential broad-spectrum antivirals; researchers are developing small-molecule candidates to boost DZIP3 activity.
